modules.title: Trading 101: How Markets Work
modules.desc: Completely free — no account needed. What a share is, how companies go public, how exchanges and prices work, and the main markets. Plain English, start from zero.

lessons.name: What a company and a share are
lessons.title: What is a company, and a share?
lessons.intro: Everything in trading starts here. Get this one idea and the rest of the market suddenly makes sense.

blocks.caption: A share is one small slice of a whole company.
blocks.alt: A company divided into many small shares, with one highlighted as yours.

blocks.text: A company is just a business that people own. When a business needs money to grow — to hire people, build products, open shops — one way to raise it is to sell small slices of ownership to the public. Those slices are called **shares** (or "stock").

If a company is divided into a million shares and you own one, you own one-millionth of that business. That entitles you to a share of its future profits (sometimes paid out as a **dividend**) and a vote on big decisions. If the business becomes more valuable, your slice becomes more valuable too — and if it struggles, your slice is worth less.
**Plain version:** a share is a tiny piece of a real company you can buy and sell. Owning shares makes you a part-owner, not a gambler on a number.

lessons.name: Going public: IPOs
lessons.title: Going public: IPOs
lessons.intro: Where do shares come from in the first place? A company decides to open its doors to the public.

blocks.caption: At the IPO the company raises cash; after that, investors trade the shares between themselves.
blocks.alt: A private company becoming publicly listed on an exchange through an IPO.

blocks.text: At first, a company's shares are usually held privately by its founders and early investors. When it decides to sell shares to the general public for the first time, that event is called an **Initial Public Offering**, or **IPO** — people say the company is "going public" or "listing".

After the IPO, the shares trade on a stock exchange, where anyone can buy them from or sell them to other investors. The company got its cash at the IPO; from then on, the day-to-day price is just people buying and selling those existing shares among themselves.
This is a key idea: **when you buy Apple shares, you're not usually buying them from Apple** — you're buying them from another investor who wants to sell.

lessons.name: Stock exchanges & market hours
lessons.title: Stock exchanges & market hours
lessons.intro: Markets aren't open 24/7 — and knowing when they open explains a lot of what you'll see.

blocks.caption: Prices can only change while the market is open — big overnight news shows up as a "gap" at the next open.
blocks.alt: A trading day bar showing the market open and close times.

blocks.text: A **stock exchange** is the organised marketplace where shares are bought and sold. The big ones you'll hear about are the London Stock Exchange (LSE), the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE) and the Nasdaq. Each lists thousands of companies.

Exchanges are only open during set hours. For example, the main US market runs roughly 9:30am to 4:00pm New York time, Monday to Friday; London runs 8:00am to 4:30pm UK time. Outside those hours the market is closed, though some products (like currencies and futures) trade nearly around the clock across global sessions.

lessons.name: Who's who in the market
lessons.title: Who's who in the market
lessons.intro: Every price is a tug-of-war between very different players. Here's who's pulling.

blocks.caption: You don't need to beat the institutions — just know they're on the other side of your trade.
blocks.alt: Retail traders, institutions, brokers and market makers.

blocks.text: Lots of different players trade at once, and it helps to know who they are:

items: **Retail traders** — everyday individuals like you, trading their own money through an app or broker.
**Institutions** — banks, pension funds and hedge funds moving very large sums.
**Brokers** — the companies that give you access to the market and place your orders (for example, a trading app).
**Market makers** — firms that always stand ready to buy and sell, which keeps the market "liquid" so your order can fill quickly.

lessons.name: How a price is set
lessons.title: How a price is actually set
lessons.intro: Nobody hands down "the price". It's simpler — and more human — than that.

blocks.caption: The price is simply where a willing buyer and a willing seller meet.
blocks.alt: Buyers and sellers meeting at an agreed price.

blocks.text: A share doesn't have an official price handed down by anyone. The price is simply **the last amount someone was willing to pay, and someone else was willing to accept**. It moves constantly as buyers and sellers change their minds.

At any moment there's a highest price buyers will pay (the **bid**) and a lowest price sellers will accept (the **ask**). When a buyer and seller agree, a trade happens and that becomes the new price. More eager buyers than sellers push the price up; more eager sellers push it down. That's supply and demand in action.

lessons.name: Reading a chart & a ticker
lessons.title: Reading a chart and a ticker
lessons.intro: A chart looks intimidating until you know the one thing it's really telling you.

blocks.caption: Up-and-to-the-right means rising; down means falling. That's enough to start.
blocks.alt: A rising price chart with a ticker symbol.

blocks.text: A **ticker** is the short code for a company — AAPL for Apple, TSLA for Tesla — usually shown next to its current price and how much it's changed today.

A **price chart** plots the price over time: time along the bottom, price up the side. Zoom out and you see the long-term trend; zoom in and you see today's wiggles. Most traders use "candlestick" charts, where each candle shows the open, high, low and close for a slice of time — but at this stage, just knowing that **up-and-to-the-right means rising, down means falling** is enough.
**Try it:** open any free charting site, type a ticker, and switch between a 1-day and a 5-year view. Seeing the same company on both is the fastest way to build intuition.

lessons.name: The main markets
lessons.title: The main markets
lessons.intro: Shares are just one item on the menu. Here's the whole menu, in plain terms.

blocks.caption: Most people focus on one or two. For now, just know the menu.
blocks.alt: Five markets: stocks, indices, forex, futures and crypto.

blocks.text: Shares are just one of several markets you can trade. In plain terms:

items: **Stocks (equities)** — slices of individual companies.
**Indices** — a basket that tracks many companies at once (e.g. the S&P 500, the FTSE 100).
**Forex (FX)** — currencies traded in pairs, like GBP/USD; the largest market in the world and open 24/5.
**Futures** — contracts to buy or sell something (an index, oil, gold) at a set date; popular with active traders and most prop firms.
**Crypto** — digital assets like Bitcoin; trades 24/7 and is highly volatile.

modules.title: Trading 201: Placing a Trade
modules.desc: Free with a free account. Order types, the bid/ask spread, going long vs short, leverage & margin, the real costs, and what moves prices.

lessons.name: Market, limit & stop orders
lessons.title: Market, limit and stop orders
lessons.intro: An order is just an instruction to your broker. Three cover almost everything you'll do — and knowing when to use each is the difference between a clean entry and a nasty surprise.

blocks.caption: Market fills now; limit waits for your price; stop fires when a level is hit.
blocks.alt: Price line showing a market order at the current price, a limit order below it, and a stop order as a trigger.

items: **Market order** — "buy/sell right now at whatever the current price is." Fast, but you don't control the exact price.
**Limit order** — "only buy at £10.00 or lower" (or "only sell at £12.00 or higher"). You control the price, but it might never fill if the market doesn't reach it.
**Stop order** — a trigger. "If the price falls to £9.00, sell me out." Used to cap a loss (a stop-loss) or to enter once a level breaks.

blocks.text: **Rule of thumb:** use limit orders when price matters more than speed, market orders when getting in or out *now* matters more, and always know where your stop is before you enter.

lessons.name: The bid, ask & spread
lessons.title: The bid, the ask and the spread
lessons.intro: There isn't one price — there are always two. The gap between them is a small cost you pay on every single trade.

blocks.caption: Buy at the ask, sell at the bid — you start each trade down by the spread.
blocks.alt: A bid price and a higher ask price with the gap between them labelled as the spread.

blocks.text: At any moment there are two prices, not one: the **bid** (the highest price buyers will pay) and the **ask** (the lowest price sellers will accept). The gap between them is the **spread**.

When you buy at market you pay the ask; when you sell at market you receive the bid. So the spread is a small, built-in cost of trading — you start every trade slightly "in the red" by the spread. Heavily traded markets (like major currencies or big stocks) have tiny spreads; thin, obscure ones have wide spreads.

lessons.name: Going long vs short
lessons.title: Going long vs going short
lessons.intro: You can profit whether a price rises or falls. Here's how both directions work — and why one of them needs extra care.

blocks.caption: Long = betting up. Short = betting down.
blocks.alt: An upward green arrow labelled long and a downward red arrow labelled short.

blocks.text: **Going long** is the familiar one: you buy expecting the price to rise, then sell higher for a profit. Buy low, sell high.

**Going short** is the mirror image: you profit when the price *falls*. Your broker effectively lets you sell first at a high price and buy back later at a lower one, pocketing the difference. It's how traders can make money in falling markets — but because a price can (in theory) rise without limit, a short that goes wrong can lose more than you put in, so it needs careful risk control.
**Key point:** prop firms and most trading platforms let you do both — being able to go short is what lets skilled traders profit in down markets too.

lessons.name: Leverage & margin
lessons.title: Leverage and margin, simply
lessons.intro: Leverage is the feature that makes small accounts interesting — and the one that wipes most of them out. Both, for the same reason.

blocks.caption: 10:1 leverage: £1,000 controls £10,000 — and multiplies every move by ten.
blocks.alt: A small margin of one thousand pounds controlling a ten thousand pound position at ten to one leverage.

blocks.text: **Leverage** lets you control a large position with a small amount of your own money. With 10:1 leverage, £1,000 of your cash can control a £10,000 position. The slice of your money set aside to hold that position is called the **margin**.

Leverage cuts both ways — it multiplies gains *and* losses by the same amount. A 5% move in your favour on 10:1 leverage is a 50% gain; a 5% move against you is a 50% loss. This is exactly why beginners blow up: not because they picked wrong, but because they used far too much leverage. Treat it as something to use sparingly, not a shortcut.

lessons.name: The real costs of trading
lessons.title: The real costs of trading
lessons.intro: Each cost is tiny. Across hundreds of trades, they decide whether a strategy is actually profitable.

blocks.caption: Know your total cost per trade — it's part of trading like a professional.
blocks.alt: Three small stacked costs: spread, commission and overnight fees.

blocks.text: Beyond the spread, watch for:

items: **Commission** — a per-trade fee some brokers charge (many are now "zero commission" but earn from the spread instead).
**Overnight / swap fees** — if you hold a leveraged position overnight, you're often charged a small financing cost each day.
**Slippage** — the difference between the price you expected and the price you actually got (next lesson but one).

blocks.text: None of these are huge on a single trade, but they add up over hundreds of trades.

lessons.name: What moves prices
lessons.title: What moves prices
lessons.intro: You don't need to predict the news — but you do need to know when it's coming.

blocks.caption: Scheduled events (like a rate decision) can move prices fast — know when they're due.
blocks.alt: A price line jumping sharply upward at the moment a news event lands.

blocks.text: Prices move when the balance of buyers and sellers shifts — and that usually happens because new information arrives. The big drivers:

items: **Company earnings** — quarterly results that beat or miss expectations move individual stocks sharply.
**Economic data** — inflation, jobs and interest-rate decisions move whole markets and currencies.
**News & sentiment** — headlines, and simple fear and greed, can move prices even without hard data.

blocks.text: You don't need to predict the news. But you should know when major scheduled events (like a central-bank rate decision) are due, because prices can move violently around them.

lessons.name: Getting filled: liquidity & slippage
lessons.title: Getting filled: liquidity and slippage
lessons.intro: The price you click and the price you get aren't always the same. Here's why — and how to keep the gap tiny.

blocks.caption: In liquid markets the gap is tiny; it widens in thin markets and around news.
blocks.alt: Expected fill price and a slightly worse actual fill price a small distance away.

blocks.text: **Liquidity** means how easily you can buy or sell without moving the price. A liquid market has lots of buyers and sellers, so your order fills instantly at the price you see. A thin market may not have anyone on the other side at your price.

**Slippage** is what happens when it doesn't fill exactly: in fast-moving or thin markets, the price you actually get can be a little worse (or occasionally better) than the price you clicked. It's usually tiny in big markets, and larger around news. Using limit orders and trading liquid markets keeps it under control.

questions.wrongFeedback: A long can only fall to zero; a short's loss grows as the price rises — and there's no ceiling.

modules.title: Trading 301: Risk & the Path to Funded
modules.desc: Free with a free account. Risk management, position sizing, stop-losses, drawdown, psychology and demo trading — and what prop firms actually are.

lessons.name: Why risk management is everything
lessons.title: Why risk management is the whole game
lessons.intro: The single idea that separates traders who last from traders who don't. It isn't about being right.

blocks.caption: Keep losses small and let wins run, and you can be wrong often and still win.
blocks.alt: Small controlled losses versus large wins keeping the account rising overall.

blocks.text: Here's the uncomfortable truth: you can be right more often than you're wrong and still lose all your money — if your losses are bigger than your wins. And you can be wrong most of the time and still profit — if you keep your losses small and let your wins run.

That's why professionals obsess over **risk**, not predictions. The first job of a trader isn't to make money; it's to **not lose too much**, so you're still around when your edge pays off. Everything else in this module builds on that idea.

lessons.name: Position sizing & the 1% rule
lessons.title: Position sizing and the 1% rule
lessons.intro: How much to risk matters more than which trade you pick. Here's the simple guardrail the pros use.

blocks.caption: Risking ~1% per trade means a losing streak stings but never wipes you out.
blocks.alt: An account bar with only 1 percent at risk on a single trade.

blocks.text: **Position sizing** is deciding how much to risk on a single trade — and it matters more than which trade you pick. A common guideline is the **1% rule**: never risk more than about 1% of your account on any one trade.

On a £10,000 account, that's £100 of risk per trade. If your stop-loss is 50 points away and each point is worth £2, that's already £100 — so that's your maximum size. Sizing this way means a losing streak stings but never wipes you out.
Traxent's **position-size calculator** does this maths for you against each prop firm's limits — but doing it by hand a few times builds the instinct.

lessons.name: Stop-losses & risk-to-reward
lessons.title: Stop-losses and risk-to-reward
lessons.intro: Decide your exit before you enter — and make sure the reward is worth the risk.

blocks.caption: At 1:2, you only need to win about a third of your trades to break even.
blocks.alt: Risking one unit to make two units, a one to two risk to reward.

blocks.text: A **stop-loss** is a pre-set exit that caps your loss if a trade goes against you. Deciding it *before* you enter — when you're calm — is what stops a small loss becoming a catastrophic one.

**Risk-to-reward (R:R)** compares what you're risking to what you stand to gain. Risk £100 to make £200 and that's 1:2. With 1:2, you only need to win about a third of your trades to break even. This is the maths behind "cut losses short, let winners run" — it's not a slogan, it's arithmetic.

lessons.name: Drawdown: how accounts blow up
lessons.title: Drawdown: how accounts blow up
lessons.intro: The maths of losses is brutal and non-obvious. Understand it and you'll protect your account by instinct.

blocks.caption: Avoiding deep drawdowns matters more than chasing big wins.
blocks.alt: Losing 50 percent needs a 100 percent gain to recover.

blocks.text: **Drawdown** is how far your account has fallen from its peak. It matters because losses and the gains needed to recover them aren't symmetric:

items: Lose 10% → you need +11% to get back to even.
Lose 50% → you need +100% just to recover.
Lose 90% → you need +900%. Practically, you're done.

blocks.text: This is why avoiding deep drawdowns matters more than chasing big wins. It's also exactly what prop firms measure — most will fail your evaluation the moment your drawdown breaches their limit, which is why Traxent scores it so heavily.

lessons.name: Psychology: FOMO, tilt & revenge
lessons.title: Psychology: FOMO, tilt and revenge
lessons.intro: Your biggest opponent isn't the market — it's the person clicking the buttons.

blocks.caption: Written rules, not willpower, are what flatten the emotional swings.
blocks.alt: An emotional, erratic decision line versus a calm rule-based line.

blocks.text: Your biggest opponent is usually yourself. Three patterns catch almost everyone:

items: **FOMO** — chasing a move you've already missed, entering late at a bad price.
**Tilt** — trading emotionally after a loss (or a win), abandoning your plan.
**Revenge trading** — trying to "win it back" immediately with a bigger, riskier trade.

blocks.text: The fix isn't willpower — it's **rules written down in advance**: your max risk, your daily loss limit, when you stop for the day. A journal that records not just the trade but how you felt is how you spot these patterns and break them.

lessons.name: Practise first: demo trading
lessons.title: Practise first: demo trading
lessons.intro: The flight simulator of trading. Use it properly and it's the cheapest lesson you'll ever get.

blocks.caption: Prove your approach is consistent on demo before real money or a paid evaluation.
blocks.alt: Practising with virtual money before risking real money.

blocks.text: **Paper (demo) trading** means placing trades with virtual money in real market conditions. It's the flight simulator of trading: you build habits, test a strategy and learn the platform without risking a penny.

Treat it seriously — use a realistic account size and follow your real rules — and it's invaluable. Treat it as a game with infinite money and it teaches bad habits. The goal is to prove, to yourself, that your approach is consistent *before* real money or a paid evaluation is on the line. This is exactly what Traxent's sim journal and readiness score are built around.

lessons.name: Prop firms & funded accounts
lessons.title: What are prop firms and funded accounts?
lessons.intro: The reason all this preparation is worth it — trading serious capital that isn't yours.

blocks.caption: Pass a rules-based evaluation and you trade the firm's capital, keeping most of the profit.
blocks.alt: A small personal account, an evaluation with rules, then a funded account with the firm's capital.

blocks.text: Most new traders don't have much capital — so a 20% year on £1,000 is only £200. **Proprietary trading firms ("prop firms")** solve this: they let you trade *their* capital and keep a large share of the profits (often 80–90%), so the same skill can earn far more.

The catch is you have to prove yourself first. You pay for an **evaluation (a "challenge")** — a demo account with strict rules: hit a profit target without breaching a daily loss limit or a maximum drawdown, often over a minimum number of days. Pass, and you're "funded" and trade for real. Fail, and you've lost the evaluation fee.
That's why preparation matters so much: **the rules, not the profit target, are what fail most people** — and they're knowable in advance. This is where the rest of Traxent picks up.

lessons.name: What is a prop firm?
lessons.title: What is a prop firm?
lessons.intro: Before you learn how to trade, understand what you're working toward. This lesson explains the prop firm model in plain English — including the specific rules you'll need to follow to pass a funded account evaluation.

blocks.text: The problem with trading your own money

Most people who want to trade face the same obstacle: **capital**. To make meaningful returns, you need a meaningful amount of money to trade with. If you have £1,000 and make a 10% return in a month, you've made £100. Impressive as a percentage — but not life-changing as an income.
The maths only works at scale. A 5% return on £100,000 is £5,000. Same skill, same percentage — very different outcome. This is where **proprietary trading firms**, or prop firms, come in.

blocks.title: Key concept
blocks.text: A prop firm provides capital to traders who can demonstrate disciplined, consistent trading. You trade their money, keep the majority of profits, and they take a cut for providing the capital and absorbing the risk.
How the evaluation works

To filter out gamblers from genuine traders, prop firms run evaluation programmes — commonly called "challenges". You pay a fee, trade a simulated account, and if you hit the profit target without breaking the rules, you receive a funded account.
Typical 2-step challenge structure

items.label: Phase 1
items.sub: Hit 10% profit target

items.label: Phase 2
items.sub: Hit 5% — prove it repeatable

items.label: Result
items.sub: Trade up to £200k · keep 80-90%

items.label: Daily loss limit
items.sub: Breach once = fail immediately

items.label: Max total loss
items.sub: Static floor — never resets

items.label: Min trading days
items.sub: Can't pass on one lucky day

blocks.text: The rules — tap each one to understand it
Most failures come not from bad trading but from breaking these rules. Click each rule below to understand exactly what it means in practice.

items.name: Daily loss limit
items.detail: Your account equity — including unrealised losses on open trades — cannot drop more than 5% below your starting balance for that day. On a £100,000 account, equity must never fall below £95,000 at any point during the session, even on an open trade that hasn't been closed yet.

items.name: Maximum total loss
items.detail: Your account balance can never fall below 90% of its starting value — ever, across the whole challenge. This is a permanent static floor. On a £100,000 account, your equity must never touch £90,000. Unlike the daily limit, this doesn't reset — it's permanent for the duration of the challenge.

items.name: Consistency rule
items.detail: On funded accounts, some firms require that no single trading day accounts for more than 30–50% of your total profit. This prevents passing by getting lucky on one big news trade. It forces genuine consistency over time — which is exactly what prop firms want to see.

items.name: Minimum trading days
items.detail: You must trade on a minimum number of days during the challenge, even if you hit the profit target early. An account that hits 10% profit on day one still can't pass — you need to prove you can trade consistently over multiple sessions, not just get lucky once.

blocks.text: Why most traders fail challenges
The failure rate on prop firm challenges is high — most estimates put it between 80–90% of first attempts. The reasons are almost never about skill or strategy.

items.label: Fail due to overtrading or revenge trading after a loss
Is all it takes to blow a challenge with one bad session
Typical challenge fee paid before you even start

blocks.title: The pattern that kills most challenges
blocks.text: A trader does well for two weeks, has one bad day, then tries to recover losses quickly by increasing position size. They breach the daily loss limit. The challenge ends. The fee is gone. This is why discipline matters more than strategy.

lessons.name: How markets move
lessons.title: How markets move
lessons.intro: Markets follow recurring patterns driven by human behaviour. This lesson covers the basics of price action — and you'll practise identifying market states directly on a real live chart.

blocks.text: Price reflects decisions, not just data

Every movement in a market price is the result of buyers and sellers agreeing — or disagreeing — on value. When more people want to buy than sell, price moves up. When more want to sell than buy, price moves down. What you see on a chart is the collective expression of confidence, fear, greed, and analysis from everyone participating in that market.

blocks.title: Key concept
blocks.text: Price action is the study of how price moves, without relying on external indicators. It asks: what is the market telling us right now, based purely on where price has been and where it is going?
The three market states

Markets spend most of their time in one of three states. Understanding which state you're in is the first question any trader should ask before placing a trade. Trading against a strong trend is one of the most common causes of losses — especially during a prop firm challenge when every loss counts against your drawdown.
The three market states

items.label: Uptrend
items.sub: Each peak above last · buyers in control

items.label: Downtrend
items.sub: Each low below last · sellers in control

items.label: Ranging
items.sub: Bouncing between levels · no winner

blocks.text: What candlesticks tell you

Most trading charts display price using **candlesticks**. Each candle represents a time period and shows four pieces of information: the opening price, closing price, highest price, and lowest price reached during that period.
Anatomy of a candlestick

items.label: Open
items.sub: Where the period began

items.label: Close
items.sub: Where the period finished

items.label: High / Low
items.sub: Shown as wicks above and below

blocks.text: A **green candle** means price closed higher than it opened — buyers won that period. A **red candle** means price closed lower — sellers won. The wicks show how far price pushed before reversing.
Timeframes — same market, different zoom levels

The same instrument looks very different depending on your timeframe. A market in a clear downtrend on the daily chart might show a short-term upward move on the 15-minute chart. Neither is wrong — they're different zoom levels of the same picture.
For prop firm challenges, most traders use the 15-minute or 1-hour chart for context, and the 5-minute chart for precise entries.

blocks.caption: A ranging market — price oscillating between support and resistance.

blocks.title: Why this matters for prop firms
blocks.text: Prop firms evaluate you on consistency — not on predicting the market perfectly. A trader who understands market structure will avoid trading against strong trends, wait for clear setups, and manage risk appropriately. That is exactly the trader a prop firm wants to fund.

lessons.name: Your first risk calculation
lessons.title: Your first risk calculation
lessons.intro: Risk management is the single most important skill in trading. This lesson shows you how to calculate exactly how much to risk on any trade — and you'll practise the calculation using a live chart setup of your choice.

blocks.text: Why risk management beats strategy

A trader with a mediocre strategy but excellent risk management will outperform a trader with a brilliant strategy and poor risk management — every time. Losses compound just as quickly as gains, and the maths of loss recovery is brutal.

items.label: Requires +11% just to get back to where you started

blocks.text: The 1% rule

Never risk more than **1% of your total account** on a single trade. On a £10,000 account, your maximum loss per trade is £100. Ten consecutive losers only costs you ~10% — recoverable. Risk 10% per trade and ten losers wipes you out entirely.

blocks.title: Key concept
blocks.text: Your risk per trade is not the same as your position size. Risk is defined by your stop loss — the point at which you accept the trade hasn't worked. Position size is calculated from your risk amount divided by your stop loss distance.
Position size formula — step by step

items.label: Step 1
items.sub: Account × risk % = £ at risk

items.label: Step 2
items.sub: |Entry − stop loss| = distance

items.label: Step 3

Risk to reward — why win rate isn't everything

Many new traders focus entirely on their win rate. But a trader who wins 40% of their trades can still be highly profitable if winners are significantly larger than losers. This is the **risk to reward ratio (R:R)**.
Break-even win rate at different R:R ratios

items.label: R:R 1:2
items.sub: Lose twice as often — still profitable

items.label: R:R 1:3

blocks.text: How this connects to prop firm rules

Every prop firm sets a maximum daily loss limit — typically 4–5% of the account. If you risk 1% per trade, you can have four or five losing trades in a row before hitting the limit. If you risk 3% per trade, two bad trades end your day. The relationship between your risk per trade and the firm's daily limit defines how much room you have to be wrong — which you will be, regularly, even as a skilled trader.

questions.text: A prop firm provides a trader with capital in exchange for what?
options: A fixed monthly fee regardless of performance
A share of the profits generated from trading their capital
Ownership of a percentage of the trader's personal assets
A guarantee that the trader will never lose money
questions.correctFeedback: Correct. Prop firms take a cut of profits — typically 10–20% — in exchange for providing the capital. The trader keeps the majority.
questions.wrongFeedback: Not quite. Prop firms make money by taking a share of profits. The ongoing model is profit sharing, not a flat fee.

questions.text: In an uptrend, which pattern do you expect to see in price movement?
options: Lower highs and lower lows
Higher highs and higher lows
Price moving sideways between two levels
Randomly alternating peaks and troughs
questions.correctFeedback: Correct. An uptrend is defined by higher highs and higher lows — each peak above the previous, each pullback stopping above the previous low.
questions.wrongFeedback: Not quite. An uptrend is identified by higher highs and higher lows. Lower highs and lower lows describe a downtrend.

questions.text: You have a £5,000 account and want to risk 1% on a trade. Your stop loss is 20 points away. What is your position size in £ per point?
options: £5 per point
£10 per point
£2.50 per point
£50 per point
questions.correctFeedback: Correct. 1% of £5,000 = £50 risk. £50 ÷ 20 points = £2.50 per point. If stopped out, you lose exactly £50.
questions.wrongFeedback: Check the maths. 1% of £5,000 = £50. Stop is 20 points away. £50 ÷ 20 = £2.50 per point.

questions.text: A trader has a risk to reward ratio of 1:3. What is the minimum win rate they need to be profitable?
options: 50% — they need to win more than they lose
40% — slightly below even
25% — they only need to win 1 in 4 trades
75% — high win rate required for this ratio
questions.correctFeedback: Correct. At 1:3 R:R, each win earns 3x what each loss costs. Win 1, lose 3, you break even. That means 25% win rate is the break-even point.
questions.wrongFeedback: At a 1:3 R:R, if you win 1 trade and lose 3, you break even (1×3 = 3×1). So 25% win rate is the minimum needed.

questions.text: What is the most common reason traders fail prop firm challenges?
options: Their trading strategy is not profitable enough
The profit targets are set too high by the firms
Poor risk management and emotional trading after losses
Lack of access to quality market data
questions.correctFeedback: Correct. Most failures come from behaviour — overtrading, revenge trading after a loss, or taking oversized positions to chase a target. Not strategy.
questions.wrongFeedback: While strategy matters, the primary cause of failures is behavioural — emotional decisions after losses, not strategy failure.

questions.text: Why do prop firms set a daily loss limit at all?
options: To cap how much profit a trader can make in one day
To protect their capital from a trader having one catastrophic day
To encourage traders to trade more frequently
questions.correctFeedback: Correct. The firm's capital is on the line — a daily loss limit stops one terrible day from doing serious damage.
questions.wrongFeedback: Think about whose money is at risk. The limit exists to protect the firm's capital from a single runaway day.

questions.text: A market keeps bouncing between a clear ceiling and a clear floor without progressing. What is this called?
options: An uptrend
A downtrend
A ranging market
A breakout
questions.correctFeedback: Correct. Price oscillating between support and resistance with no direction is a range.
questions.wrongFeedback: When price bounces between the same two levels without making progress, it's ranging — not trending.

questions.text: You risk £50 on a trade with a stop 25 points away. What is your position size per point?
options: £2 per point
£4 per point
£25 per point
£0.50 per point
questions.correctFeedback: Correct. £50 ÷ 25 points = £2 per point.
questions.wrongFeedback: Divide the cash risk by the stop distance: £50 ÷ 25 = £2 per point.

questions.text: Which of these best describes a funded trader's ongoing deal with a prop firm?
options: Keep 100% of profits but pay a monthly fee
Keep the majority of profits, with the firm taking a small share
Salary plus bonuses set by the firm
Keep 25% of profits, the firm keeps 75%
questions.correctFeedback: Correct. Typical splits give the trader 80-90% of profits; the firm keeps the rest.
questions.wrongFeedback: Funded traders usually keep the lion's share — often 80-90% — while the firm takes the remainder.

questions.text: FTMO's evaluation uses a static maximum drawdown. What does 'static' mean here?
options: The limit trails your equity peak upward as you profit
The limit is measured from your starting balance and never moves
The limit resets at the start of each trading day
The limit only applies during news events
questions.correctFeedback: Correct. A static drawdown is anchored to the starting balance — profits don't drag the floor up behind you.
questions.wrongFeedback: Static means fixed from the starting balance. A limit that follows your equity peak is a TRAILING drawdown.

questions.text: Apex Trader Funding uses a trailing drawdown. Why is that generally harder to manage than a static one?
options: It only counts closed trades
The floor rises with your equity peak, so early profits can be given back and still breach it
It is always a larger percentage than static limits
questions.correctFeedback: Correct. As your equity climbs, the drawdown floor climbs with it — give back early gains and you can fail while still above your starting balance.
questions.wrongFeedback: Trailing means the floor follows your equity peak up. That's what catches traders out after a strong start.

questions.text: Which habit most directly prepares you for ANY firm's evaluation, regardless of its specific rules?
options: Trading only during the London session
Maximising trade frequency to hit targets faster
Consistent risk per trade with a hard stop on every position
Focusing on one instrument forever
questions.correctFeedback: Correct. Fixed risk plus a hard stop keeps you inside daily loss and drawdown limits automatically — the rules most evaluations fail people on.
questions.wrongFeedback: The universal preparation is risk discipline: consistent risk per trade and a hard stop, which keeps you inside every firm's loss limits.

lessons.name: Bull flag and bear flag
lessons.title: Why patterns work
lessons.intro: Chart patterns are not magic. They work because markets are made of humans — and humans react to price levels in predictable, repeatable ways. Understanding the psychology behind patterns separates traders who use them well from those who chase every candle.

blocks.text: Markets are driven by human psychology

Every chart pattern is a visual representation of a battle between buyers and sellers. When you see a flag pattern, you're seeing a market that surged in one direction, paused while participants caught their breath, then continued. The pattern works not because of the shape, but because of what the shape tells you about who is in control and what they're likely to do next.
This is why the same patterns appear repeatedly across different instruments, timeframes, and decades. Human psychology doesn't change. Fear and greed look the same in 1990 as they do today.

blocks.title: Key concept
blocks.text: A chart pattern is a shortcut for reading market psychology. The shape tells you the story of the battle between buyers and sellers — and gives you a probabilistic idea of what happens next.
Patterns only work in context

The biggest mistake beginners make is trading patterns in isolation. A bull flag in a downtrend is a much weaker signal than a bull flag in an established uptrend. Context — the broader market structure from Module 1 — always takes priority over the pattern itself. Before you look for patterns, ask: what is the trend?

lessons.title: Bull flag & bear flag
lessons.intro: The flag pattern is one of the most reliable continuation patterns in trading. It appears across every market and every timeframe — and once you can identify it, you'll see it everywhere.

blocks.text: What a flag looks like

A flag has two parts: the **pole** and the **flag**. The pole is a sharp, strong move in one direction — driven by buyers (bull flag) or sellers (bear flag). The flag is the consolidation that follows — a slow, orderly pullback against the direction of the pole.

The key insight: the pullback is **not a reversal**. It's the market pausing before continuing in the original direction. Weak participants are shaken out. Strong participants use the pullback to enter at a better price.
Bull flag anatomy

items.label: The pole
items.sub: Strong momentum · large candles

items.label: The flag
items.sub: Orderly decline · small candles

items.label: The breakout
items.sub: Breaks flag high with momentum

blocks.text: Bull flag
CONTINUATION · BULLISH
Forms after a strong upward move. Price consolidates in a slight downward channel, then breaks out to the upside.
Entry:
Break above the upper trendline of the flag with a strong candle close
Stop loss:
Below the low of the flag consolidation
Target:
Measure the pole height and project from the breakout point
Avoid:
Flags where the pullback retraces more than 50% of the pole
Bear flag
CONTINUATION · BEARISH
The exact mirror of the bull flag. After a strong downward move, price consolidates in a slight upward channel before breaking down.
Entry:
Break below the lower trendline of the flag
Stop loss:
Above the high of the flag consolidation
Target:
Pole height projected downward from the breakout
Avoid:
Flags that drift sideways rather than slightly against the trend

lessons.title: Inside bar
lessons.intro: The inside bar is a compression pattern — price is coiling before its next move. One of the cleanest patterns to trade because the rules are simple and risk is clearly defined.

blocks.text: What an inside bar is

An inside bar is any candle whose **high and low are completely contained within the range of the previous candle**. The previous candle — the mother bar — represents a period of price discovery. The inside bar represents a pause, a compression of energy before the next move.
Inside bar structure

items.label: Mother bar
items.sub: Sets the range · defines high and low

items.label: Inside bar
items.sub: Both high and low inside mother bar

items.label: Breakout
items.sub: Break above = bullish · break below = bearish

blocks.text: Inside bar breakout
CONTINUATION OR REVERSAL
The inside bar is direction-neutral — it signals compression, not direction. The direction comes from context and from which side it breaks.
Entry:
Break of the mother bar high (bullish) or low (bearish) with a candle close outside
Stop loss:
Opposite side of the mother bar
Best context:
After a trend, at a key support or resistance level
Avoid:
Inside bars in choppy, ranging markets with no clear directional bias

blocks.title: Why this works for prop firm challenges
blocks.text: Inside bars give you an extremely tight stop loss — you're risking the range of the mother bar, often just a few points or pips. This means very precise risk per trade, directly supporting daily loss limits.

lessons.name: VWAP reclaim
lessons.title: Break of structure & VWAP reclaim
lessons.intro: Two of the most widely used concepts by professional and prop firm traders. Break of structure tells you when a trend has genuinely changed. VWAP tells you who is in control of the session.

blocks.text: Break of structure (BOS)

From Module 1 we know an uptrend is defined by higher highs and higher lows. A **break of structure** occurs when that sequence breaks — when price makes a lower low in an uptrend, or a higher high in a downtrend. This marks the moment when the balance of power shifts.
Break of structure — bullish and bearish

items.label: Bullish BOS
items.sub: Price closes above previous swing high

items.label: Bearish BOS
items.sub: Price closes below previous swing low

items.label: Key rule
items.sub: Close beyond the level — wicks don't count

blocks.title: Real world example
blocks.text: EUR/USD has been making lower highs and lower lows for two months — a clear downtrend. Then price makes a higher high, closing above the previous swing high. That is a bullish BOS. The trader does not immediately go long, but they stop looking for short entries and start watching for confirmation of the new direction.
VWAP — Volume Weighted Average Price

VWAP is the average price at which a security has traded throughout the day, weighted by volume. It is the most widely watched intraday level by institutional traders — banks, hedge funds, and prop firms all use it as a reference point.

**Price above VWAP means buyers have been in control for the session. Price below means sellers have.** A VWAP reclaim — where price dips below it then closes back above — is a strong signal that buyers have reasserted control.
VWAP reclaim
INTRADAY · MOMENTUM SIGNAL
When price dips below VWAP but then closes back above it, buyers are stepping in at the average institutional price — a bullish signal.
Setup:
Price above VWAP, dips below briefly, then reclaims with a strong close above
Entry:
On the candle close back above VWAP, or a small pullback after the reclaim
Stop loss:
Below the low of the VWAP reclaim candle
Best context:
During trending sessions, not in choppy pre-market periods

questions.text: What is the most important factor to check before trading any chart pattern?

The pattern must have occurred at least three times before
Volume must be higher than average when the pattern forms

The base and the breakout
The consolidation and the reversal

Both the high and low must be within the previous candle's range
The inside bar must close above the midpoint of the mother bar
Volume must decrease on the inside bar
questions.correctFeedback: Correct. Both the high and low must be contained within the mother bar. That is the sole defining requirement.
questions.wrongFeedback: Not quite. The only requirement for a valid inside bar is that both the high and low are within the mother bar's range.

The instrument is overvalued and should not be traded

questions.wrongFeedback: Not quite. Price above VWAP means buyers have been in control of the session — a bullish indication.

options: When two moving averages cross each other
When multiple independent signals align at the same price level
When a pattern appears on multiple instruments simultaneously
When trading volume confirms a price move
questions.correctFeedback: Correct. Confluence is the coming together of multiple independent signals at the same level — increasing the probability that the trade works.

options: A steep collapse retracing most of the pole
A tight, orderly drift sideways or slightly down on falling volume
A wide, volatile range larger than the pole itself
questions.correctFeedback: Correct. A healthy flag is a calm, shallow consolidation — the market catching its breath, not reversing.
questions.wrongFeedback: The flag should be tight and orderly, drifting sideways/slightly against the trend on reduced volume.

options: The trend has definitively reversed
The market is compressing — a breakout of the mother bar's range often follows
Volume is guaranteed to spike
It signals institutional selling
questions.correctFeedback: Correct. Inside bars mark compression; the break of the mother bar's high or low is the tradeable event.
questions.wrongFeedback: An inside bar is compression, not reversal — the signal comes when price breaks the mother bar's range.

questions.text: What confirms a bullish break of structure (BOS)?
options: Price touching the previous swing high
Price closing decisively above the previous swing high
Price closing above VWAP
Two consecutive green candles
questions.correctFeedback: Correct. A BOS needs a decisive close through the prior swing high — a wick alone isn't conviction.
questions.wrongFeedback: A touch or a wick isn't enough; structure breaks when price CLOSES through the previous swing high.

options: Price loses VWAP, then reclaims it and holds above
Price never touches VWAP all session
VWAP crosses above the daily open
Price closes exactly on VWAP

questions.wrongFeedback: The reclaim pattern is: price loses VWAP, takes it back, and holds above. The hold is the confirmation.

questions.text: Why does a pattern aligned WITH the higher-timeframe trend have better odds?
options: Patterns only form in trends
You're joining the dominant order flow instead of fighting it
Lower timeframes are always noise
It guarantees the trade wins
questions.correctFeedback: Correct. Trading with the higher-timeframe direction means the bigger flow is behind your trade — nothing is guaranteed, but odds improve.
questions.wrongFeedback: Alignment matters because the dominant flow is behind you. No guarantee — just better odds than fighting the tide.

questions.text: You spot a textbook bull flag, but your prop firm evaluation has a daily loss limit you're close to breaching. What's the disciplined play?

Skip or defer the trade; protecting the evaluation comes first
Double the size to win back the day's losses
questions.correctFeedback: Correct. No single pattern outranks survival. Near the daily limit, the evaluation IS the trade.
questions.wrongFeedback: Pattern quality never outranks the daily loss limit — breach it and the evaluation is gone. Protect the account first.

questions.text: A flag's consolidation retraces 80% of its pole on rising volume. What should you conclude?
options: A stronger breakout is coming
The pattern is compromised — deep retrace and rising counter-volume aren't flag behaviour
It has become an inside bar
Nothing changes; entry rules are identical
questions.correctFeedback: Correct. Deep retracement with growing opposing volume says distribution, not rest — the flag thesis is broken.
questions.wrongFeedback: A healthy flag retraces shallowly on FALLING volume. 80% retrace on rising volume breaks the pattern's logic.

lessons.name: Stop loss placement strategies
lessons.title: Stop loss placement
lessons.intro: Where you place your stop loss is as important as where you enter. A stop placed too tight gets hit by normal market noise. A stop placed too wide means you're risking too much. This lesson covers the principles of logical stop placement.

blocks.text: The purpose of a stop loss

A stop loss has one job: to exit the trade at a predetermined price when the reason you entered is no longer valid. It is not there to prevent losses — losses are part of trading. It is there to ensure that any single loss is **controlled and predictable**.

The worst type of stop loss is one placed at a round number or at a fixed point distance from entry without any relationship to the market structure. A good stop loss is placed at a level where, if price reaches it, the original trade idea is clearly wrong.

blocks.title: Key concept
blocks.text: Your stop loss should be placed at the point where the market tells you your trade idea is wrong — not at the point where your pain tolerance runs out.
Three logical stop loss placements

blocks.text: The buffer principle

Markets are not precise. Price often moves a few points beyond a level before reversing — this is called a **wick** or a **liquidity sweep**. Placing your stop exactly at a swing low means a single wick can stop you out even if your trade direction is correct. A small buffer — 1-3 points or pips beyond the level — helps avoid being stopped out by noise while still exiting if the level is genuinely broken.

blocks.title: Prop firm specific
blocks.text: On futures accounts with trailing drawdown (Apex, MFFU), be especially careful about stop placement. A wide stop combined with multiple positions can consume your trailing drawdown quickly on a volatile day. Tight, logical stops protect both your trade and your drawdown buffer.

lessons.name: Risk to reward — the long game
lessons.title: Risk to reward — the long game
lessons.intro: Understanding risk to reward is what separates traders who think about each individual trade from traders who think about their edge over hundreds of trades. This lesson shows you why a 40% win rate can be more profitable than a 70% win rate.

blocks.text: Expectancy — what matters over time

Every trader has a **win rate** (how often they are right) and an **average risk to reward ratio** (how much they make per winner relative to how much they lose per loser). These two numbers together determine whether a trading approach is profitable over time — regardless of any individual trade result.

The formula: **Expectancy = (Win rate × Average win) − (Loss rate × Average loss)**. If this number is positive, the approach is profitable over time. If it's negative, no amount of good luck makes it sustainable.

lessons.title: How accounts blow up
lessons.intro: Understanding the specific ways trading accounts get destroyed is just as important as knowing how to build them. This lesson covers the four most common account killers — all of which are preventable.

blocks.text: The four account killers
In almost every prop firm challenge failure, one of these four patterns is present. They're not about strategy — they're about psychology and discipline.
The four account killers

items.label: 1. Revenge trading
items.sub: Taking bigger trades after a loss to "get it back"

items.label: 2. Overtrading
items.sub: Taking setups that don't meet your criteria

items.label: 3. Moving stops
items.sub: Moving stop loss further away when trade goes wrong

items.label: 4. No daily loss limit
items.sub: No personal rule to stop trading after losing X%

blocks.text: The revenge trading spiral

Revenge trading is the single biggest cause of prop firm challenge failures. The pattern is consistent: trader loses a trade, feels frustrated, increases position size on the next trade to recover quickly, loses again, increases further, blows the daily loss limit. The entire sequence can happen in under an hour.

The solution is simple but hard to implement under pressure: **set a personal daily loss limit below the firm's limit**. If you lose 3% in a day, stop trading. Walk away. Come back tomorrow. The challenge has no time limit. The account does not care that you had a bad morning. Tomorrow is always a fresh start.
How professionals handle losses

Professional prop firm traders treat a losing day the same way a professional golfer treats a bad hole: they don't try to make it back on the next hole with a reckless shot. They play the next hole as they would any other — with the same process, the same criteria, the same discipline.
This is the mental model that separates traders who consistently pass challenges from those who pass once, then fail repeatedly.

blocks.title: The rule that saves most challenges
blocks.text: Set your personal daily stop-loss at 2.5–3% — well below the firm's 4–5% limit. If you hit it, stop for the day. This one rule prevents revenge trading from ending your challenge, and leaves you with enough buffer that a bad morning can't cost you everything.

Just below the low of the flag consolidation, with a small buffer
At the exact point where the flag started forming

questions.text: A trader has a 40% win rate but an average risk to reward ratio of 1:3. Are they profitable?

Yes — at 1:3 R:R, a 40% win rate produces positive expectancy

Higher than the firm's limit — take more risk for more reward

Beyond the structure that invalidates the setup — e.g. below the swing low
At the day's low, whatever the setup
Wherever it caps risk at exactly £100

questions.wrongFeedback: No daily cap doesn't mean no discipline: the 4% EOD trail makes your end-of-day equity the critical number.

blocks.text: The FTMO evaluation structure

FTMO uses a two-step evaluation. Phase 1 — the Challenge — requires a 10% profit target. Phase 2 — Verification — requires 5%. Both phases share the same loss limits. Importantly, there is **no time limit** on either phase. You can take as long as you need, which removes one of the biggest failure triggers: forcing trades near an artificial deadline.

blocks.text: The floating loss rule — most misunderstood

Most traders understand the 5% daily limit in concept. What catches people is how it's calculated: FTMO measures your **equity including unrealised floating losses on open positions**, from your account balance at midnight Prague time (CET/CEST).

This means: if you start the day at £100,000 and open a position that goes −£5,100 floating — even though you haven't closed the trade — you've breached the daily limit. The trade is still live. The challenge is over. Even if it later recovers.

blocks.title: The floating loss trap
blocks.text: If your stop loss is correctly placed and sized at 1% risk, a single trade can never breach the daily limit on its own. The trap only catches traders who trade too large, move stops wider, or don't use stops at all. Proper position sizing from Module 3 is your protection.
Static drawdown — why it gets easier over time

FTMO's maximum loss limit is **static**: on a £100,000 account, the floor is always £90,000. No matter how much profit you make, the floor never moves up. This is a significant advantage — as your account grows from trading profits, the buffer between your current balance and the floor gets larger, not smaller. Once you're at £105,000, you have £15,000 of buffer above the £90,000 floor.
The 1-step FTMO — the Best Day rule

FTMO also offers a 1-step challenge. It is faster but adds an additional constraint: your single most profitable day cannot exceed **50% of your total Positive Days' Profit**. This prevents traders passing via one lucky news event. For traders with consistent day-to-day performance, the 1-step can be faster. For traders with variable daily results, the 2-step is more forgiving.

lessons.name: Apex and MFFU — key differences

blocks.text: Side-by-side comparison
The critical difference — static vs trailing drawdown

FTMO's drawdown is **static**: the floor is set at the start and never moves. This means the buffer between your current balance and the floor grows as you profit. The risk of breaching actually decreases over time.

Apex uses an **intraday trailing drawdown**: the floor follows your peak equity in real time, including unrealised gains on open trades. If your account grows to £107,000 intraday on a trade that hasn't closed, the floor may have moved up. If the trade then pulls back, you're closer to the floor than you expected — even though your closed balance is still higher than when you started.

lessons.name: Building a consistent trading plan

lessons.intro: Everything in this course leads here. A trading plan is not a strategy — it is the framework within which your strategy operates. Without one, even a profitable strategy fails under the emotional pressure of a real challenge.

blocks.text: What a trading plan actually is

A trading plan is a set of pre-committed decisions made when you're calm and thinking clearly — so you don't have to make them in the moment when emotions are high. It covers what you trade, when you trade, how much you risk, when you stop for the day, and how you review your performance.

blocks.title: The key insight
blocks.text: The purpose of a trading plan is to remove decisions from the heat of the moment. If your plan says "stop after two losses in a day", you don't need to decide whether today's third setup is "different enough" to override the rule. The decision is already made. Discipline is easier when the rules are pre-set.

questions.text: You're on a £100,000 FTMO account. Your account balance at midnight was £103,000 (from previous profits). What is your maximum loss allowed today?
options: £5,000 — always 5% of the original starting capital
£5,150 — 5% of yesterday's closing balance
£10,300 — 10% of yesterday's balance
£3,000 — the remaining buffer to the static floor
questions.correctFeedback: Correct. FTMO calculates the daily loss limit from your balance at midnight CET — not the original starting capital. At £103,000 closing balance, 5% = £5,150. Your daily limit grows slightly as your account grows.
questions.wrongFeedback: FTMO recalculates the daily loss limit from your balance at midnight each day. If your account closed at £103,000, your daily limit is 5% of that = £5,150. Not 5% of the original £100,000 starting capital.

questions.text: Which firm uses an intraday trailing drawdown — meaning the floor follows your peak equity in real time, including unrealised gains on open trades?
options: FTMO (static drawdown)
MyFundedFutures Core (EOD trailing)
Apex Trader Funding (intraday trailing)
FundedNext Futures (EOD trailing)
questions.correctFeedback: Correct. Apex uses an intraday trailing drawdown that follows peak equity including floating gains in real time. FTMO uses a static floor. MFFU and FundedNext use end-of-day trailing — the floor only updates once per day at market close.
questions.wrongFeedback: Apex Trader Funding uses intraday trailing drawdown. It follows your peak equity in real time, including unrealised profits. This is distinct from FTMO (static), MFFU (EOD trailing), and FundedNext (EOD trailing).

questions.text: During a prop firm challenge, you've hit your personal daily loss limit of 2.5% by midday. A very high-probability setup then appears. What do you do?
options: Take the setup — it's too good to miss
Take half size — 0.5% risk instead of 1%
Close the platform — the rule applies even to good setups
Check the firm's official limit first — 2.5% might not be the real limit
questions.correctFeedback: Correct. Personal daily rules are only meaningful if they're absolute. The moment you make exceptions for 'good setups', the rule stops functioning. Every trader who broke their rules did so because the setup looked too good to skip. Stop when you hit the limit.
questions.wrongFeedback: Personal daily loss limits exist precisely to prevent this situation. If you allow exceptions for 'good setups', the rule becomes meaningless. The answer is always: stop trading when you hit your personal limit, regardless of what the next setup looks like.

questions.text: A simulated trading week shows a trader with a 43% win rate but a net positive result. What does this tell you about their trading approach?
options: Nothing — a 43% win rate is always unprofitable
They must be using very high risk per trade to compensate
They are using a risk to reward ratio greater than 1:1, so losing more often than winning is still profitable
This is impossible — you need 50%+ win rate to make money
questions.correctFeedback: Correct. A 43% win rate is profitable at 1:2 R:R (break-even is 34%). Winning less than half your trades while still making money is the expected outcome when targeting rewards that are larger than your risks. This is why R:R matters more than win rate.
questions.wrongFeedback: At 1:2 R:R, break-even win rate is 34%. A 43% win rate is above the break-even point — profitable. You don't need a 50%+ win rate when your winners are larger than your losers. Win rate alone tells you very little without the R:R context.

questions.text: What are the two trading plan violations that caused the most damage in the simulated challenge week?
options: Trading too many instruments and using the wrong timeframe
Forcing a trade with no clear setup, then revenge trading at 3× normal risk
Holding trades overnight and trading during news events
Taking too many trades on Monday and not enough on Thursday
questions.correctFeedback: Correct. The two Wednesday violations were: (1) entering a trade with 'no clear setup' — a setup criteria violation, and (2) revenge trading at 3% risk instead of 1% — a risk management violation. These two decisions turned a manageable bad day into the worst session of the week.
questions.wrongFeedback: The Wednesday violations were specifically: first, entering a forced trade with no clear setup (setup criteria violation), and second, a revenge trade at 3× normal risk (risk management violation). These are the most common and most damaging trading plan failures in prop firm challenges.

questions.text: FTMO's Two-Phase evaluation measures maximum drawdown how?
options: Trailing your equity peak intraday
Static from the starting balance
Reset monthly
End-of-day trailing
questions.correctFeedback: Correct. FTMO's classic challenge uses a static max drawdown anchored to the starting balance.
questions.wrongFeedback: FTMO's standard challenge drawdown is STATIC — measured from the starting balance, not trailing.

questions.text: Topstep's consistency rule caps your best single day at roughly what share of total profit?
questions.correctFeedback: Correct. Around 50% — no single day may dominate your profit, forcing genuine day-to-day consistency.
questions.wrongFeedback: Topstep's consistency threshold is about 50% of total profit from any single day.

questions.text: Apex's consistency rule is stricter than most at around 30%. What behaviour is it designed to prevent?
options: Trading too many contracts at once
Passing the evaluation with one lucky outsized day instead of repeatable skill
Holding trades over the weekend
Trading outside US market hours
questions.correctFeedback: Correct. Consistency rules exist so one jackpot day can't carry an evaluation — the firm wants repeatable performance.
questions.wrongFeedback: The 30% cap stops a single windfall day from carrying the whole evaluation — firms fund repeatability, not luck.

questions.text: MyFundedFutures measures its 3% drawdown at end of day. Compared with an intraday trailing measure, what does this allow?
options: Nothing different — they're identical
Your equity can dip intraday without breaching, as long as it recovers by the close
Unlimited intraday losses with no consequences ever
questions.correctFeedback: Correct. EOD measurement forgives intraday dips that recover before the close — only the closing equity is tested.
questions.wrongFeedback: End-of-day measurement means the breach test happens at the close — intraday dips that recover don't count.

questions.text: Why do most firms impose a minimum number of trading days?
options: To collect more commission
To prove performance across different market conditions rather than one session
Because regulators require it
To keep servers busy
questions.correctFeedback: Correct. Minimum days force the evaluation across varied conditions — one hot session proves little.
questions.wrongFeedback: Minimum-day rules exist to see you perform across different days and conditions, not a single lucky session.

questions.text: A solid challenge trading plan should specify which of these BEFORE any trade is taken?
options: Only the profit target
Entry criteria, risk per trade, daily stop, and which sessions you trade
Just the instruments you like
The firm's payout schedule
questions.correctFeedback: Correct. Entries, fixed risk, a personal daily stop and defined sessions — decided calmly in advance, followed mechanically.
questions.wrongFeedback: A plan is the full ruleset: entry criteria, risk per trade, personal daily stop and trading windows — all pre-decided.

questions.text: You're comparing two firms: one with a 5% daily loss limit + static 10% max, another with no daily limit + 4% EOD trailing. Your trading style has volatile intraday swings that usually recover. Which fits better, and why?
options: The first — daily limits suit volatile styles
The second — EOD measurement forgives intraday swings that recover by the close
Neither can work for this style
Both are identical in practice
questions.correctFeedback: Correct. If your equity dips intraday but recovers, EOD measurement is far more forgiving than an intraday daily limit.
questions.wrongFeedback: Match the rule to the style: volatile-but-recovering intraday equity survives EOD measurement, but can breach an intraday daily cap.

lessons.name: The trader's brain under pressure
lessons.title: The trader's brain under pressure
lessons.intro: You can know every rule and pattern and still fail a challenge — because trading is a performance done under stress. This lesson explains what actually happens in your head when money is on the line, and why your worst decisions feel the most justified.

blocks.text: Why smart people make terrible trades

When you place a trade, you are not a calm analyst. You are a nervous system reacting to perceived gain and loss. Decades of behavioural research show two forces dominate: **loss aversion** — losses hurt roughly twice as much as equivalent gains feel good — and **the fight-or-flight response**, which floods your body with cortisol and adrenaline the moment a position moves against you.

Under that chemistry, the part of your brain responsible for patient, rule-based decisions (the prefrontal cortex) gets quieter, and the reactive, threat-driven part gets louder. You do not feel irrational in that moment — you feel **certain**. That certainty is the trap.

blocks.title: Key concept
blocks.text: Discipline is not about feeling calm. Everyone feels fear and greed. Discipline is the ability to follow your plan **despite** what you feel. The goal is not to remove emotion — it is to remove emotion's authority over your actions.
The three emotional states that cost money
Almost every blown challenge traces back to one of three states. Learning to name the state you are in is the first step to interrupting it.
The three costly states

items.label: Fear
items.sub: Skip valid setups · cut winners early · move stops away

items.label: Greed
items.sub: Oversize · add to winners blindly · ignore the plan

items.label: Tilt
items.sub: Trade to recover a loss · abandon rules entirely

blocks.text: The cost of one emotional decision

In a prop firm challenge, the asymmetry is severe. Weeks of disciplined trading can be erased by a single tilt session. The maths of drawdown is unforgiving, which is exactly why emotional control is a hard requirement, not a soft skill.

items.label: How much more a loss hurts than an equal gain feels good (loss aversion)
Is all it takes for a tilt spiral to breach a daily loss limit
Of challenge failures are behavioural, not strategic

blocks.title: Spot the state
blocks.question: You take a loss right at your stop. Within 30 seconds you are sizing up a new trade that is not on your plan, telling yourself you can "make it back quickly." Which state are you in?

options.label: Fear — you are protecting capital
options.feedback: This is not fear. Fear makes you hesitate; here you are rushing to act to recover a loss — that is tilt.

options.label: Greed — you spotted a great opportunity
options.feedback: This is not greed. The motive is recovering a loss, not pressing an advantage — that is tilt.

options.label: Tilt — you are trading to recover the loss
options.feedback: Correct. The instant urge to place an unplanned trade right after a loss, framed as "making it back", is textbook tilt. The disciplined response is to step away, not to act.

blocks.title: The tell
blocks.text: The phrase "make it back" is the single most reliable warning sign in trading. The market does not know or care that you just lost. A recovery trade is not analysis — it is your nervous system trying to undo pain. The correct response is almost always to stop trading for the session.

lessons.name: Tilt, FOMO and revenge trading
lessons.title: Tilt, FOMO and revenge trading
lessons.intro: These three patterns destroy more funded accounts than any bad strategy ever could. This lesson breaks down how each one works, how to recognise it in yourself in real time, and the specific circuit-breaker for each.

blocks.text: Tilt — the recovery spiral

Tilt is borrowed from poker: a state of emotional frustration that leads to reckless decisions. In trading it usually starts with a loss that feels unfair — a stop hunt, a news spike, a trade that was "right" but stopped out. The frustration drives a bigger, faster trade to recover, which often loses, which deepens the tilt. Within an hour a disciplined trader can breach a daily limit they have respected for weeks.

blocks.title: Circuit-breaker for tilt
blocks.text: A hard, pre-committed rule: **two losses in a row, or down 2% on the day, means you are done trading for that session.** Not "one more trade." Done. Close the platform. The rule must be set before you trade, because in the moment your judgement is compromised.
FOMO — the fear of missing out

FOMO is the urge to chase a move that is already running, because watching it go without you feels like losing money you never had. Chasing means entering late, with a wide or absent stop, far from any logical invalidation level. The risk-to-reward is terrible precisely because the easy part of the move is already gone.
A planned entry vs a FOMO chase

items.label: Planned
items.sub: Enter near support · tight stop · clear invalidation

items.label: FOMO
items.sub: Enter extended · no logical stop · poor R:R

blocks.text: Revenge trading — making it personal

Revenge trading treats the market as an opponent that owes you. It is tilt aimed at a specific instrument or a specific loss. The tell is emotional language: "this pair always does this to me", "I'm getting my money back from gold today." The market is not an adversary. It is indifferent. Any sentence that frames a trade as payback is a signal to stop.

blocks.title: FOMO under challenge pressure
blocks.question: NQ runs 80 points in your intended direction while you were away from the desk. You feel the urge to jump in so you do not "miss the rest." You are two days into a challenge with a 4% daily limit. What is the disciplined action?

options.label: Enter now at market — the trend is clearly strong
options.feedback: Chasing the move is the FOMO trap: late entry, no logical stop, bad R:R. Wait for a pullback or skip it.

options.label: Enter now but with double size to make up lost ground
options.feedback: Double size on a chased entry is the fastest route to a daily-limit breach. Wait for a defined entry instead.

options.label: Wait for a pullback to a level with a defined stop — or skip it
options.feedback: Correct. The easy part of the move is gone. Waiting for a pullback to a level gives you a defined stop and acceptable risk-to-reward — and skipping it entirely is a perfectly good answer.

blocks.title: Catching tilt early
blocks.question: You have lost two trades in a row this morning, both at your stop. Your pre-set rule is "two losses = stop for the session." You still feel sharp and you see another setup forming. What do you do?

options.label: Take the setup — feeling sharp means the rule does not apply today
options.value: take the setup — feeling sharp means the rule does not apply today

options.label: Take it at half size as a compromise
options.feedback: Half size is still breaking the rule. A pre-committed limit only works if you do not bargain with it. Stop for the session.

options.label: Honour the rule — stop for the session, review tomorrow
options.feedback: Correct. The rule exists precisely for moments when you feel fine and want to override it. Honouring it on the hard day is the entire point of having it.

blocks.title: Why "I feel sharp" is the trap
blocks.text: Rules exist for the version of you that is compromised — and that version always believes it is the exception. The entire value of a pre-committed rule is that you follow it on the day you least want to. The moment you negotiate with the rule, you no longer have one.

lessons.name: Building a discipline system
lessons.title: Building a discipline system
lessons.intro: Willpower is unreliable — it fades exactly when pressure peaks. Professionals do not rely on willpower; they rely on systems that make the disciplined choice the default. This lesson gives you a concrete framework you can use from your next session.

blocks.text: Rules beat willpower

The trader who says "I'll just be more disciplined next time" will fail again, because they are relying on a resource that depletes. The trader who writes down three hard rules and follows them mechanically will outperform them — not because they are calmer, but because they removed the decision from the moment of stress.

blocks.title: Key concept
blocks.text: Make decisions when you are calm, so you do not have to make them when you are not. Every rule you set in advance is a decision your stressed self does not get to override.
The pre-trade checklist
A 15-second checklist inserts a deliberate pause between impulse and action. It does not slow good trades down — it stops bad ones.
A minimal pre-trade checklist

items.label: 1 · Setup
items.sub: A defined setup — not a feeling

items.label: 2 · Stop
items.sub: A logical level, set before entry

items.label: 3 · Size
items.sub: Calculated, not eyeballed

blocks.text: Daily guardrails
Beyond the per-trade checklist, set hard session limits before the day begins. These are the rails that keep a bad day from becoming a blown challenge.
Example daily guardrails

items.label: Loss cap
items.sub: Well inside the firm's daily limit

items.label: Streak rule
items.sub: No "one more" after two losers

items.label: Win rule
