blocks.text: The role of the journal

You cannot fix what you do not measure. A journal that records not just entries and exits but your **emotional state** and whether you followed your rules turns vague feelings into data. Over time you will see your own patterns — the time of day you tilt, the instrument that baits you, the setup you overtrade. Module 6 covers exactly how to build that review habit, and the Traxent journal and readiness tracker are designed to log this for you automatically.

blocks.title: Traxent note
blocks.text: Process over outcome. A trade that followed every rule and still lost was a **good** trade. A trade that broke your rules and happened to win was a **bad** trade — it just rewarded the wrong behaviour. Judge yourself on the process, and the outcomes follow.

lessons.name: Module 5 quiz

questions.text: What is the best working definition of trading discipline?
options: Never feeling fear or greed while trading
Following your plan despite what you feel in the moment
Trading only when you feel completely calm
Avoiding losses entirely through careful analysis
questions.correctFeedback: Correct. Everyone feels emotion. Discipline is acting on your plan rather than your feelings — removing emotion's authority, not the emotion itself.
questions.wrongFeedback: Discipline is not the absence of emotion — you will always feel it. It is following your plan despite what you feel.

questions.text: A trader takes a loss and immediately enters an unplanned trade to 'make it back fast.' What is happening?
options: Smart capital recovery
Tilt / revenge trading
Disciplined risk management
A valid FOMO entry
questions.correctFeedback: Correct. The phrase 'make it back' after a loss, driving an unplanned trade, is the clearest signal of tilt. The right move is to stop.
questions.wrongFeedback: An unplanned trade driven by a desire to recover a loss is tilt. 'Make it back' is the warning phrase to watch for.

questions.text: Why are pre-committed rules (like 'two losses = stop for the day') more effective than willpower?
options: Willpower is unlimited, so rules are just a backup
Rules remove the decision from the moment when judgement is compromised
Rules guarantee you never have a losing day
Willpower works better the more stressed you are
questions.correctFeedback: Correct. You set rules while calm so your stressed self cannot override them. Willpower depletes exactly when pressure peaks.
questions.wrongFeedback: The value of a rule is that it removes the decision from the stressed moment. Willpower fades precisely when you need it most.

questions.text: You're chasing an 80-point move that already ran without you. What's the core problem with entering now?
options: The trend is too strong to trade
You'd be entering extended, far from any logical stop, with poor R:R
Large moves always reverse immediately
There is no problem — strong trends are free money
questions.correctFeedback: Correct. Chasing means a late entry with no logical invalidation and poor risk-to-reward — the defining flaw of FOMO trades.
questions.wrongFeedback: The problem is entry quality: chasing leaves you extended with no logical stop and bad R:R. Wait for a pullback or skip it.

questions.text: How should you judge whether a single trade was 'good' or 'bad'?
options: By whether it made or lost money
By whether you followed your plan and rules
By how big the profit was
By whether other traders agreed with it
questions.correctFeedback: Correct. Process over outcome. A rule-following trade that lost was good; a rule-breaking trade that won was bad — it rewarded the wrong behaviour.
questions.wrongFeedback: Judge the process, not the outcome. A losing trade that followed your rules was good; a winning trade that broke them was bad.

questions.text: After two quick losses you feel a surge to 'win it back' immediately with a bigger trade. What is this pattern, and what's the correct response?
options: Revenge trading — step away or drop to minimum size per your written rules
Momentum trading — increase size while volatility is high
Intuition — act on it quickly before it fades
questions.correctFeedback: Correct. That urge is revenge trading. The written rule — stop or size down — exists precisely because you can't reason well in that state.
questions.wrongFeedback: The 'win it back' urge after losses is revenge trading, and the answer is pre-written rules: stop for the day or cut size.

questions.text: Why do written rules beat willpower for trading discipline?
options: Willpower is infinite if you train it
Decisions made calmly in advance don't have to be re-made under stress, when your judgement is worst
Rules are only for beginners
Because firms require documentation
questions.correctFeedback: Correct. The whole point of pre-commitment: the decision is already made, so the stressed version of you just follows it.
questions.wrongFeedback: Under pressure, judgement degrades. Rules move the decision to when you were calm — that's why they beat in-the-moment willpower.

questions.text: FOMO entries typically happen at what point in a move?
options: Before the move starts
Early, at the planned trigger
Late, after the move is extended — at the worst available price
Only in ranging markets
questions.correctFeedback: Correct. FOMO strikes after a move is obvious — which is exactly when the price is worst and the risk is largest.
questions.wrongFeedback: Fear of missing out kicks in once a move is well underway — so FOMO entries are late, extended, and poorly priced.

questions.text: You've hit your personal daily loss stop but 'feel certain' about one more setup. Under a prop firm's daily loss limit, taking it risks what?
options: Nothing — feelings are data
Turning a controlled losing day into a breached evaluation, since tilt-driven certainty is exactly when errors compound
A margin call from your broker
Missing tomorrow's session
questions.correctFeedback: Correct. The 'certain' feeling after losses is tilt wearing a disguise — and near a daily limit it can end the whole evaluation.
questions.wrongFeedback: That certainty after losses IS tilt. One more trade near the daily limit risks the evaluation itself, not just one loss.

questions.text: Which is a sign of tilt AFTER a winning streak?
options: Reviewing the winners in your journal
Oversizing and loosening entry criteria because you feel invincible
Taking a planned break
Reducing size to protect profits
questions.correctFeedback: Correct. Winner's tilt: euphoria loosens rules and inflates size. Streaks in either direction distort judgement.
questions.wrongFeedback: Tilt cuts both ways — after wins it shows up as oversizing and sloppy entries born of overconfidence.

questions.text: A useful journal entry for psychology tracking records what alongside the trade details?
options: The weather that day
Your emotional state and whether the trade followed your plan
Your favourite instrument only
Nothing extra — numbers are enough
questions.correctFeedback: Correct. Emotion + plan-adherence per trade is what reveals patterns like tilt and FOMO in review.
questions.wrongFeedback: To catch behavioural leaks you need the feelings and plan-match logged with each trade — that's what review mines later.

questions.text: What's the disciplined structure for a trading day, start to finish?
options: Open charts and react to whatever moves
Pre-market plan → trade only planned setups → post-market review and journal
Trade all sessions to maximise opportunity
Check P&L constantly and adjust size to feelings
questions.correctFeedback: Correct. Plan, execute the plan, review the execution — the loop that compounds discipline.
questions.wrongFeedback: The professional day is a loop: plan before, execute only the plan during, review honestly after.

lessons.name: The numbers that actually matter
lessons.title: The numbers that actually matter
lessons.intro: Most traders track the wrong number: profit and loss. P&L is an outcome, not a cause. This lesson covers the handful of metrics that actually describe whether you have an edge — and lets you compute your own expectancy.

blocks.text: Win rate is not your edge

New traders obsess over win rate, but a 70% win rate with tiny winners and huge losers loses money, while a 35% win rate with large winners and small losers prints. What matters is the combination of how often you win and how big your wins are relative to your losses. That combination has a name: **expectancy**.

blocks.title: Key concept — expectancy
blocks.text: Expectancy is the average amount you can expect to win (or lose) per trade, in units of risk (R). The formula: **(Win% × Avg win in R) − (Loss% × Avg loss in R)**. A positive expectancy means that, repeated enough times, the system makes money. A negative one means it bleeds — no matter how good any single trade felt.
Thinking in R

The cleanest way to measure trading is in **R** — multiples of the amount you risked. If you risk 1% and make 2%, that is +2R. If you risk 1% and lose it, that is −1R. Measuring in R removes account size and position size from the picture and lets you compare every trade on equal footing.
Two traders, same P&L, very different edge

Trader B wins less than half the time but has 8x the expectancy. Over 100 trades, Trader A nets +5R while Trader B nets +40R. Same markets — completely different outcome, driven by the size of winners relative to losers.

blocks.title: Sample size matters
blocks.text: A positive expectancy over 10 trades tells you almost nothing — variance dominates small samples. You need 50+ trades before the number means much, and you must keep risk consistent for R to be comparable. This is exactly the kind of consistency a prop firm is testing for.

lessons.name: Journaling that changes behaviour
lessons.title: Journaling that changes behaviour
lessons.intro: A journal that only records entries and exits is a spreadsheet. A journal that records your reasoning and emotional state is a mirror — and it is the single highest-leverage habit a developing trader can build.

blocks.text: What to actually log

Price data is the least useful thing in a trade journal — your platform already has it. The value is in the context only you can capture: **why** you took the trade, whether it matched your plan, how you felt, and what you did when it moved. That is the data that reveals your leaks.
Fields that change behaviour

items.label: Setup
items.sub: Named setup, or "off-plan"

items.label: Plan match
items.sub: Did you follow your rules?

items.label: Emotion
items.sub: Calm · FOMO · tilt · bored

items.label: Result
items.sub: +/− multiples of risk

items.label: Management
items.sub: Held stop? Moved it? Cut early?

items.label: Lesson
items.sub: What would you repeat or change?

blocks.text: The 'plan match' column is the whole game
If you log only one extra field, log whether the trade followed your plan. Over a few weeks you can sort your trades into four boxes — and the pattern that emerges is almost always the same.
The four boxes

items.label: On-plan · won
items.sub: Your edge working as designed

items.label: On-plan · lost
items.sub: A good trade with a bad outcome

items.label: Off-plan · lost
items.sub: Easy to see and cut

items.label: Off-plan · won
items.sub: Rewards the wrong behaviour

blocks.title: The most dangerous box
blocks.text: Off-plan trades that **win** are the ones that destroy traders, because the profit teaches your brain that breaking the rules pays. The journal is what lets you label that win as a bad trade and refuse to repeat it. Without the record, you just remember the money.

blocks.title: Reading your own journal
blocks.question: Your journal shows that 80% of your losing R comes from trades you marked "off-plan", and your on-plan trades have a positive expectancy. What is the highest-leverage change?

options.label: Find a new strategy — your edge is not good enough
options.feedback: A new strategy would throw away an edge that already works. The leak is off-plan trades — cut those.

options.label: Increase size on on-plan trades to grow faster
options.feedback: Increasing size magnifies both the edge and the leak. Fix the off-plan leak first, then consider sizing.

options.label: Simply stop taking off-plan trades — your edge already works
options.feedback: Correct. Your edge already works on-plan; the entire loss is coming from off-plan trades. Cutting them is the single highest-leverage change — no new strategy needed.

blocks.title: Traxent note
blocks.text: The Traxent sim journal and readiness tracker are built to capture exactly these fields — plan match, emotion, result in R — and surface the patterns automatically, so you get the feedback loop without maintaining a spreadsheet by hand.

lessons.name: The weekly review loop
lessons.title: The weekly review loop
lessons.intro: Logging trades is input. The review is where the learning happens. This lesson gives you a repeatable weekly routine that turns a pile of trades into one or two concrete changes — the loop that separates traders who improve from traders who just accumulate screen time.

blocks.text: Why weekly, not daily

Daily review is too noisy — a single day is mostly variance. Weekly gives you enough trades to see a pattern without so many that the signal blurs. The aim of each review is modest and specific: leave with **one thing to keep doing and one thing to change**. Not ten. One of each is enough to compound.

items.label: 1 · Measure
items.sub: Update your numbers for the week

items.label: 2 · Sort
items.sub: On/off-plan vs won/lost

items.label: 3 · Find
items.sub: Where did the losing R come from?

items.label: 4 · Decide
items.sub: A single, specific rule tweak

items.label: 5 · Commit
items.sub: Make it the focus of next week

items.label: 6 · Repeat
items.sub: Small weekly gains stack up

blocks.text: Make changes one at a time

If you change five things at once and your results improve, you have no idea which change helped — and you cannot keep what worked. Change one variable, give it a meaningful sample of trades, then measure. This is the same discipline a scientist uses, and it is why traders who review methodically pull away from those who tinker constantly.

blocks.title: Choosing the change
blocks.question: Your weekly review shows your expectancy is positive overall, but every Friday afternoon you give back most of the week's gains in over-traded, off-plan positions. What is the single best change for next week?

options.label: Rebuild your whole strategy from scratch
options.feedback: Rebuilding everything is overkill and untestable. Change one variable that targets the Friday leak.

options.label: Add one rule: stop trading Friday after midday
options.feedback: Correct. One specific, testable rule that targets the exact leak the data revealed. Measure it next week, then keep or adjust.

options.label: Trade bigger earlier in the week to bank more before Friday
options.feedback: Sizing up earlier ignores the actual leak and adds risk. Target the Friday over-trading with one rule.

blocks.title: Readiness, not hope
blocks.question: You want to buy a prop firm challenge. Which signal best tells you that you are actually ready, rather than just hopeful?

options.label: You feel confident and have had a few good days recently
options.feedback: Confidence is not readiness. You need a meaningful sample showing positive expectancy within the firm's limits.

options.label: A 50+ trade sample shows positive expectancy while staying inside the firm's daily and max-loss limits
options.feedback: Correct. Readiness is evidence: a meaningful sample with positive expectancy that respected the firm's limits. That is what tells you to buy a challenge.

options.label: You hit the profit target once in a demo last week
options.feedback: One target hit is a small sample and could be luck. Readiness needs a consistent, rule-respecting sample.

blocks.title: This is what Traxent measures
blocks.text: Readiness is evidence, not a feeling: a sample of trades with positive expectancy that would have respected a firm's specific rules. The Traxent readiness tracker scores exactly that against each firm, so you buy a challenge when the data says go — not when hope does.

lessons.name: Module 6 quiz

questions.text: Why is win rate a poor measure of a trading edge on its own?
options: Win rate is impossible to calculate accurately
A high win rate with small winners and big losers can still lose money
Win rate only matters for futures, not forex
Prop firms ignore win rate entirely
questions.correctFeedback: Correct. Edge is win rate combined with the size of winners vs losers — i.e. expectancy. A 70% win rate with tiny wins and big losses loses money.
questions.wrongFeedback: Win rate alone is misleading: you also need the size of wins vs losses. Together they form expectancy.

questions.text: A system wins 40% of the time, with average wins of 2.5R and average losses of 1R. What is its expectancy?
options: −0.10R (loses over time)
+0.40R (profitable over time)
Exactly break-even
questions.correctFeedback: Correct. (0.4 × 2.5) − (0.6 × 1) = 1.0 − 0.6 = +0.40R per trade. Positive expectancy.
questions.wrongFeedback: Work it through: (0.4 × 2.5) − (0.6 × 1) = +0.40R. Positive expectancy despite a sub-50% win rate.

questions.text: In a trade journal, which single extra field is most likely to change your behaviour?
options: The exact entry and exit price
Whether the trade followed your plan ('plan match')
The time the market opened
The broker's spread at entry
questions.correctFeedback: Correct. 'Plan match' lets you sort trades into on/off-plan and see that most losses are off-plan — the clearest, most actionable leak.
questions.wrongFeedback: Price data is already in your platform. Logging whether the trade followed your plan is what reveals your real leaks.

questions.text: Why is an off-plan trade that WINS considered dangerous?
options: It isn't — a win is always good
The profit teaches your brain that breaking your rules pays off
Winning trades are taxed more heavily
It always reverses the next day
questions.correctFeedback: Correct. An off-plan win rewards rule-breaking behaviour, making you more likely to repeat it. The journal lets you label it a bad trade.
questions.wrongFeedback: An off-plan win reinforces the wrong behaviour — your brain remembers the money, not the broken rule. That's why it's dangerous.

questions.text: What best indicates you are genuinely ready to buy a prop firm challenge?
options: You feel confident after a few good days
A 50+ trade sample with positive expectancy that stayed within the firm's daily and max-loss limits
You hit the profit target once in a demo
A friend passed the same firm's challenge
questions.correctFeedback: Correct. Readiness is evidence — a meaningful sample showing a positive, rule-respecting edge against that specific firm's limits.
questions.wrongFeedback: Readiness is data, not a feeling or a single result. You want a 50+ trade sample with positive expectancy inside the firm's limits.

questions.text: Expectancy per trade combines which ingredients?
options: Win rate alone
Win rate, average win size and average loss size
Number of trades and account size
Profit factor and leverage
questions.correctFeedback: Correct. Expectancy = (win% × avg win) − (loss% × avg loss) — what a trade earns you on average.
questions.wrongFeedback: Expectancy needs all three: how often you win, how big wins are, how big losses are.

questions.text: Why do traders measure results in R (risk units) instead of pounds?
options: It sounds more professional
It normalises results across position sizes and account growth, exposing the true quality of decisions
Brokers require it
It hides losses
questions.correctFeedback: Correct. A +2R trade is a +2R trade at any account size — R strips money noise off the decision quality.
questions.wrongFeedback: R-multiples make trades comparable regardless of size or account — the decision quality shows through.

questions.text: Your journal shows most losing R comes from trades tagged 'off-plan', while on-plan trades are profitable. The highest-leverage fix is…
options: A new strategy
Stop taking off-plan trades — the edge already works
Increase size on everything
Trade more instruments
questions.correctFeedback: Correct. The edge exists; the leak is discipline. Cutting off-plan trades is the single highest-leverage change.
questions.wrongFeedback: The data says the strategy works ON plan — the fix is eliminating off-plan trades, not finding a new edge.

questions.text: An off-plan trade that WINS should be journalled as…
options: A success to repeat
A bad trade that happened to pay — because it rewards rule-breaking
Proof the plan is too strict
Nothing unusual
questions.correctFeedback: Correct. Winning off-plan trades are the dangerous ones — the profit teaches your brain that breaking rules pays.
questions.wrongFeedback: Process over outcome: an off-plan winner is still a bad trade, and labelling it that way is what stops the habit.

questions.text: What belongs in a weekly review loop?
options: Only the week's P&L
Sort trades into on/off-plan × won/lost, find the biggest leak, set ONE change for next week
Re-watching every chart tick by tick
Comparing yourself to other traders
questions.correctFeedback: Correct. The four-box sort plus a single concrete change — small, compounding improvements beat grand overhauls.
questions.wrongFeedback: The loop is: categorise (on/off-plan vs won/lost), identify the one biggest leak, commit to one change. Repeat weekly.

questions.text: With a 40% win rate, which average R:R makes you profitable?
options: Any ratio — 40% is unprofitable
questions.correctFeedback: Correct. At 1:2, break-even is ~33%, so 40% wins is comfortably profitable. Win rate means nothing without R:R.
questions.wrongFeedback: At 1:2 R:R the break-even win rate is about 33% — so 40% is profitable. Win rate alone tells you little.

questions.text: For a prop evaluation with a ~50% consistency rule, which journal metric deserves special attention?
options: Best single trade ever
The share of total profit coming from your best single day
Number of instruments traded
Average hold time
questions.correctFeedback: Correct. If one day dominates your profit you'd fail the consistency check — tracking that share tells you before the firm does.
questions.wrongFeedback: Consistency rules test day-to-day evenness: watch what fraction of total profit your best day represents.

lessons.intro: 5 questions on metrics, journaling and the review loop. You need 80% to pass and complete the learning path.

lessons.name: Confirm your best-fit firm
lessons.title: Confirm your best-fit firm
lessons.intro: You've done the work and your readiness score says you're prepared. This module is the bridge from practising in Traxent to trading for real — choosing a platform, practising on it in demo, connecting it to Traxent so your real performance scores itself, and stepping into an evaluation with live data behind you.

blocks.title: Before you start
blocks.text: This onboarding is designed for traders who have reached 85%+ readiness on a tracked firm. Not there yet? Keep logging trades on the readiness tracker first.

Open the readiness tracker and check the best-matched firm panel. It ranks at least 16 firms against how you actually trade — your drawdown discipline, consistency and trading days — and names the one whose rules fit you best.

lessons.name: Choose a platform you can practise on
lessons.title: Choose a platform you can practise on — and that Traxent syncs with

blocks.text: Pick a trading platform that (a) matches your firm's asset class and (b) Traxent can read, so your trades flow in automatically. Start in **demo / paper mode** — it behaves like the real thing but risks nothing, and it's the cleanest way to rehearse the exact firm rules before you pay an evaluation fee.

items: Futures (Apex, Topstep, MyFundedFutures, Tradeify…): Tradovate, NinjaTrader or Rithmic.
Forex / indices (FTMO, FundedNext, FXIFY…): cTrader or MetaTrader 4/5.

blocks.text: On the Integrations page, connect your account. Traxent only ever **reads** your closed trades and equity curve to score them — it never places trades or touches your funds. Your real performance then updates your readiness score and journal automatically.

lessons.name: Attempt the evaluation & track funded phase
lessons.title: Attempt the evaluation — then track the funded phase

blocks.text: When your real, connected data holds above the firm's rules, buy the evaluation with confidence. After you pass, keep the account connected: Traxent tracks payout readiness and drawdown discipline on funded capital, so staying funded becomes as measurable as getting funded.
